subject: Career
title: Financial Planning for Career Transitions
description: One-minute skill: Financial Planning for Career Transitions.

hook.text: She wanted to switch careers but had three months of savings. That's a transition without a parachute.

buildup.text: Financial runway determines how much time you can afford to transition, retrain, and find the new role.

discovery.text: Experts recommend 6-12 months of expenses saved before making a major career change.

twist.text: Income doesn't have to go to zero. Part-time work, freelancing, or consulting bridges the gap.

climax.text: Calculate your 'burn rate' — monthly expenses minus any income. That's your transition clock.

punchline.text: Freedom to choose requires financial runway. Build it first.

quiz.question: How much savings do experts recommend before a major career transition?

details.summary: Financial planning for career transitions involves calculating a runway of savings, reducing expenses, and creating interim income streams. Most experts recommend six to twelve months of living expenses saved before making a major move.
details.whyItMatters: Financial stress impairs decision-making at exactly the moment you need it most. A solid financial plan turns a leap of faith into a calculated risk.
takeaways: Calculate your monthly burn rate and multiply by your transition timeline
Reduce fixed expenses before the transition to extend your runway
Freelancing or part-time work during transition preserves savings

faq.question: How much money should you save before changing careers?
faq.answer: A general rule is six to twelve months of essential living expenses, plus any retraining costs. If your transition is a pivot within a related field, six months may suffice. A full industry leap to an entry-level position may require twelve months or more.

faq.question: Is it ever wise to change careers without a financial safety net?
faq.answer: Only if you have a signed offer in the new field or a partner whose income covers household expenses. Without a safety net, financial desperation forces you to accept the first available option rather than the right one.
